title: Time, range and impact velocity
learning_outcomes: Find projectile flight time from vertical motion.
Find horizontal range using the shared time.
Determine impact speed and direction from perpendicular velocity components.
prior_knowledge_summary: Students can resolve initial velocity and analyse independent horizontal and vertical component motions.
Students know horizontal velocity is constant and vertical acceleration is g downward when air resistance is negligible.
Students can use signed constant-acceleration equations and interpret velocity as a vector.
new_learning: Obtain the shared flight time from the vertical equation and then use it horizontally.
Calculate range from constant horizontal velocity.
Calculate the final vertical velocity and recombine it with the horizontal component.
State impact direction as an angle below or above the horizontal.
knowledge_boundary: Use only ideal two-dimensional projectile motion with constant downward g and negligible air resistance. Do not optimise range or introduce drag.

visual_rules.reason: Six visuals distribute the clock, range, component, vector and checking ideas across the lesson.
visual_rules.style: hand-drawn teacher sketches with basic annotations

blocks.title: Which calculation must come first?
body: A rescue robot launches a supply capsule across a gap. You know its launch velocity and the lower landing height. Should you calculate the horizontal distance first or the falling time first? Predict the useful starting direction.
Horizontal distance needs time. The vertical motion contains gravity and the height change, so it gives the clock. Once time is known, the horizontal calculation becomes simple.

figure.purpose: Create the need to solve the vertical motion before the horizontal range.
figure.brief: Teacher sketch of a capsule crossing a gap to a lower platform, with an unknown-time clock icon beside the vertical drop and an unknown-range bracket horizontally.
figure.alt_text: A capsule travels to a lower platform with unknown flight time and horizontal range.

blocks.title: Let the vertical motion set the clock
body: Choose upward as positive. List vertical data only: u_y, a_y = -9.81 m s^-2 and vertical displacement s_y. Then solve for the positive time that reaches the landing height.

Formula to remember: s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2. In the vertical column, s_y = u_y t + \frac{1}{2}a_y t^2. If the projectile lands below launch, s_y is negative. A quadratic may give two roots, but only a time consistent with the stated interval is physical.

figure.purpose: Make the signed vertical setup and physical root choice explicit.
figure.brief: Annotated vertical sign diagram beside a compact knowns table and a quadratic timeline showing rejection of a negative-time root.
figure.alt_text: Upward-positive vertical data lead to a positive physical flight time while a negative root is rejected.

blocks.title: Use that same time to find range
body: A capsule is launched horizontally at 8.0 m s^-1 from a platform 5.0 m above its landing level. Vertically, u_y = 0, s_y = -5.0 m and a_y = -9.81 m s^-2. So -5.0 = \frac{1}{2}(-9.81)t^2, giving t = 1.01 s.
Formula to remember for constant velocity: s = vt. Horizontally, s_x = v_x t = 8.0 times 1.01 = 8.08 m. The time came from vertical motion and was then carried unchanged into the horizontal line.

figure.purpose: Show the required vertical-then-horizontal calculation order.
figure.brief: Two-column worked layout with an arrow carrying t = 1.01 s from the vertical column into the horizontal range column.
figure.alt_text: A vertical calculation finds time, which is transferred to the horizontal range calculation.

blocks.title: Build the impact velocity from its components
body: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement. At impact, horizontal velocity is still v_x = u_x. Find the final vertical component with a vertical equation.

Formula to remember: v = u + at. Vertically, v_y = u_y + a_y t. Formula to remember: v^2 = u^2 + 2as can instead find v_y when time is unnecessary. Here velocities are in m s^-1, acceleration is in m s^-2, displacement is in m and time is in s.

The impact speed is the magnitude of the right-triangle resultant: v = sqrt(v_x^2 + v_y^2). The angle to the horizontal satisfies tan theta = |v_y|/|v_x|. State whether it is below or above the horizontal.

figure.purpose: Connect signed final components to impact speed and direction.
figure.brief: Impact-point velocity triangle with rightward v_x, downward v_y, resultant v and angle below horizontal, beside Pythagoras and tangent labels.
figure.alt_text: Perpendicular impact velocity components combine into a resultant speed directed below horizontal.

blocks.title: Do not combine too early
body: It is tempting to put the launch speed straight into a vertical equation or to use the range as vertical displacement. That feels efficient because the projectile has one path, but the equations describe one chosen direction at a time.
Resolve first. Use u_y and s_y vertically to get time or v_y. Use v_x horizontally to get range. Recombine v_x and v_y only when the question asks for the final speed or direction.

figure.purpose: Contrast a mixed-quantity setup with the correct component workflow.
figure.brief: Crossed-out single equation mixing total u and horizontal s beside a clean flow: resolve, vertical clock, horizontal range, final vector triangle.
figure.alt_text: An incorrect mixed-direction equation is contrasted with the correct component-by-component workflow.

blocks.title: Same-level angled projectile
body: A ball is launched at 20.0 m s^-1, 30 degrees above horizontal, and lands at launch level. Take upward as positive.
Resolve: u_x = 20.0 cos 30 degrees = 17.3 m s^-1 and u_y = 20.0 sin 30 degrees = 10.0 m s^-1.
Vertical flight sets the clock: 0 = u_y t - 1/2 gt^2. Apart from t = 0, t = 2u_y/g = 2.04 s.
Shared time gives range x = u_x t = (17.3)(2.04) = 35.3 m.
Impact speed is sqrt(17.3^2 + 10.0^2) = 20.0 m s^-1. Direction is tan^-1(10.0/17.3) = 30 degrees below horizontal.

figure.purpose: Make the reasoning in same-level angled projectile visible.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn teacher-sketch summary with a positive axis, compact values, arrows, and only the labels needed for the reasoning.
figure.alt_text: Teacher sketch for same-level angled projectile.

blocks.title: Unequal launch and landing levels
body: A stone is launched at 16.0 m s^-1, 25 degrees above horizontal, from a ledge 12.0 m above the ground.
Resolve: u_x = 14.5 m s^-1 and u_y = 6.76 m s^-1.
For the ground, vertical displacement is s_y = -12.0 m. Solve -12.0 = 6.76t - 4.905t^2. The positive root is t = 2.40 s.
Final vertical velocity is v_y = 6.76 - (9.81)(2.40) = -16.8 m s^-1.
Impact speed is sqrt(14.5^2 + 16.8^2) = 22.2 m s^-1. Direction is tan^-1(16.8/14.5) = 49.2 degrees below horizontal.
Check: v_y^2 = u_y^2 + 2a_y s_y gives the same 16.8 m s^-1 vertical speed.

figure.purpose: Make the reasoning in unequal launch and landing levels visible.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn teacher-sketch summary with a positive axis, compact values, arrows, and only the labels needed for the reasoning.
figure.alt_text: Teacher sketch for unequal launch and landing levels.

blocks.title: Check the landing answer
body: Use three quick checks. Flight time must be positive. Range must point in the horizontal direction of launch. At a landing below the path, the final vertical velocity should point downward.

Now the opening capsule can be solved in a fixed order: resolve the launch, use vertical displacement to find time, use horizontal motion to find range, find the final vertical component, and combine components for impact speed and direction. The separate stories meet only at the shared time and final vector.

figure.purpose: Provide a compact end-to-end procedure and physical checks.
figure.brief: Five-step hand-drawn flowchart ending in an impact triangle, with small check marks for positive time, horizontal direction and downward final vertical component.
figure.alt_text: A projectile solution flow runs from resolving velocity to checking the impact vector.

concepts_taught: Vertical motion determines projectile flight time.
The same flight time gives horizontal range from constant horizontal velocity.
Impact velocity is the vector sum of final horizontal and vertical components.
Impact direction must be stated relative to the horizontal.
misconceptions_addressed: Range should be calculated before time.
Total launch speed can be inserted into a vertical equation.
Impact speed is found by adding component magnitudes directly.
skills_students_can_now_use: Calculate projectile flight time from vertical motion.
Calculate horizontal range using the shared time.
Calculate final vertical velocity with signed data.
Determine impact speed and angle from perpendicular components.
Check physical signs, directions and roots.
next_lesson_can_assume: Students can complete ideal projectile calculations for time, range and impact velocity.
Students can select and apply component equations in a mixed kinematics problem.
Students can state a resultant velocity magnitude and direction.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Students can optimise range with launch angle.
Students have studied later-topic forces or energy unless supplied.
